adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:30 — [P1 confidence 100] "for i = 0, 1000 do" the redirect graph remains unbounded when payload eviction caps only the sorted set, so a trace with more than 1,001 chained span IDs resolves later descendants to an intermediate deleted key and splits one segment across multiple buffers.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real consistency issue. The diff shows: 1) Loop limit reduced from 10000 to 1000 (line 30), 2) Span count capped at 1000 via zpopmin (lines 55-57), 3) But the redirect hash (main_redirect_key) that maps span_ids to set_span_ids is NOT bounded. When zpopmin evicts spans from the sorted set, their entries in the redirect hash remain. If a trace has >1000 spans with deep parent chains, new spans may follow redirect chains to span_ids whose data was evicted, causing them to be stored in separate buffers. The redirect graph and the sorted set are not kept in sync, which can split segments.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:53 — [P1 confidence 100] "span_count = redis.call(\"zunionstore\", set_key, 2, set_key, parent_key)" Redis ZUNIONSTORE defaults to SUM for duplicate members, so an at-least-once replay already present in the canonical set has its end-timestamp score doubled during merge and is retained ahead of genuinely newer spans while those newer spans are evicted.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real issue. Looking at the diff in add-buffer.lua, lines 47-48 and 53-54 show zunionstore being used to merge sorted sets. ZUNIONSTORE with default AGGREGATE SUM will add scores together when the same member exists in multiple sets. Since the score represents end_timestamp_precise (as shown in buffer.py line 196-198 where zadd uses end_timestamp_precise as the score), if a span is replayed and already exists in the set, its timestamp score would be doubled. Then at lines 61-63, zpopmin removes the lowest-scored spans when count exceeds 1000. This means spans with artificially inflated scores (from duplicate processing) would be retained while legitimately newer spans with correct timestamps could be evicted. This is a correctness bug in at-least-once delivery scenarios.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:62 — [P2 confidence 100] "if span_count > 1000 then" the hard-coded insertion cap disconnects retention from SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans, so every non-default buffer configuration silently enforces 1,000 while exposing a different configured limit that no code uses.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a hardcoded limit of 1000 in the Lua script (line 62: 'if span_count > 1000 then') that enforces span retention. Looking at buffer.py, there's a 'max_segment_spans' attribute used in the SpansBuffer class (visible in the removed code around line 446-452 that checked 'if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans'). The Lua script's hardcoded 1000 limit operates independently of this Python configuration, meaning any configured max_segment_spans value other than 1000 would be inconsistent with the Lua enforcement. This is a real configuration disconnect bug.

src/sentry/api/paginator.py:821 — [P2 confidence 100] "class OptimizedCursorPaginator(BasePaginator):" this out-of-scope 91-line clone creates a second copy of BasePaginator.get_result that already diverges from the shared pagination semantics, so delete paginator.py:821-911 together with organization_auditlogs.py:70-83 and cursors.py:26-27 or future paginator fixes will leave the audit-log branch behaviorally stale.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:62 — [P2 confidence 100] "if span_count > 1000 then" the insertion cap bypasses the existing SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans setting, so every non-default configured maximum is silently unenforced after this change.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that in add-buffer.lua, a hardcoded limit of 1000 spans is enforced (lines 57-59: 'if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)'). adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/spans/buffer.py:197 — [P1 confidence 100] "p.zadd(" reuses each existing `span-buf:s:*` key while changing its Redis type from Set to Sorted Set, so any in-flight segment written by the previous version makes new ingestion fail with WRONGTYPE throughout a rolling deployment until that key expires.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a clear change from Redis Set operations (sadd, scard, sscan, sunionstore) to Sorted Set operations (zadd, zcard, zscan, zunionstore) on the same key pattern 'span-buf:s:{project_and_trace}:*'. In buffer.py line 197, the code changes from 'p.sadd(set_key, ...)' to 'p.zadd(set_key, ...)'. During a rolling deployment, old instances will write Sets while new instances write Sorted Sets to the same keys. Redis will throw WRONGTYPE errors when trying to perform Set operations on a Sorted Set key or vice versa. This is a real deployment compatibility bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/spans/buffer.py:434 — [P1 confidence 100] "p.zscan(key, cursor=cursor, count=self.segment_page_size)" reads every queued segment exclusively as a Sorted Set, so pre-deployment Set-backed segments fail flushing with WRONGTYPE and expire without ever being emitted.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a migration from Redis Sets (SADD, SCARD, SSCAN, SUNIONSTORE) to Sorted Sets (ZADD, ZCARD, ZSCAN, ZUNIONSTORE). In buffer.py line 434, the code now uses p.zscan() to read segment data. However, any segments that were written before this deployment using SADD (Sets) will still exist in Redis as Set data types. When zscan is called on a Set key, Redis returns a WRONGTYPE error because zscan only works on Sorted Sets. This means pre-existing segments written as Sets cannot be flushed and will expire without being processed, causing data loss during the deployment transition.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/spans/buffer.py:197 — [P1 confidence 100] "p.zadd(" Redis rejects this command with WRONGTYPE whenever a still-live span-buf:s key was created as a Set by the previous version, so a normal rolling deployment fails ingestion for in-flight segments.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a change from Redis Set commands (sadd, scard, sscan, sunionstore) to Sorted Set commands (zadd, zcard, zscan, zunionstore) in buffer.py. During a rolling deployment, old code may have created keys using Set commands (sadd), and when new code tries to use Sorted Set commands (zadd) on those same keys, Redis will return a WRONGTYPE error because you cannot use sorted set operations on a key that was created as a regular set. This is a real deployment compatibility issue that would cause ingestion failures for in-flight segments.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/api/paginator.py:882 — [P2 confidence 100] "results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])" an optimized request carrying a negative cursor offset takes this branch and Django rejects the negative QuerySet slice with an uncaught ValueError, returning a raw 500.

Django QuerySets do not support negative slicing and will raise a ValueError (AssertionError in some versions) with message like 'Negative indexing is not supported.' This is a real bug - the code path is reachable when a user passes optimized_pagination=true and has superuser/global_access permissions, and provides a cursor with a negative offset.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:53 — [P1 confidence 100] "span_count = redis.call(\"zunionstore\", set_key, 2, set_key, parent_key)" replaying a span whose parent key redirects into a canonical set places the same payload in both inputs, so Redis SUM doubles its timestamp score and the 1,000-span eviction silently drops a genuinely newer span instead.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that replaying a span causes the same payload to appear in both inputs to zunionstore, doubling the score. However, looking at the Lua script, the zunionstore operations merge different keys: (1) set_key with span_key, and (2) set_key with parent_key. The span_key and parent_key are different keys based on different span IDs. The script uses 'unlink' to delete the source keys after merging, preventing duplicate entries. Additionally, zunionstore with sorted sets uses the SUM aggregation by default, but if the same member exists in both sets, it would need to be the exact same payload - which would only happen if the same span was somehow added twice to different keys. The finding's scenario about 'replaying a span whose parent key redirects into a canonical set' is not clearly demonstrated by the diff, and the redirect mechanism (lines 30-38) handles span ID redirects, not payload duplication. The claim is speculative and not verifiable from the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:62 — [P2 confidence 100] "if span_count > 1000 then" configuring SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans above 1,000 still evicts every member beyond this hard-coded threshold, silently discarding spans that the configured runtime limit permits.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a hardcoded limit of 1000 in the Lua script (line 62: 'if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)'). Looking at buffer.py, there's a configurable 'max_segment_spans' parameter used elsewhere in the codebase (visible in the removed code around line 446-452 that checked 'if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans'). The Lua script now enforces a hardcoded 1000 limit that will silently discard spans regardless of what max_segment_spans is configured to. This is a real inconsistency where the runtime configuration is ignored in favor of a hardcoded value.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:30 — [P2 confidence 100] "for i = 0, 1000 do" a trace whose redirect chain exceeds 1,001 hops stops resolution at an intermediate key and silently flushes one logical segment as multiple partial segments.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the loop limit was reduced from 10000 to 1000 at line 30. The original code had a comment explaining 'theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly.'
